Three settings shape a session before you type the first request: how much the agent may do before it stops to ask, whether it plans before it edits, and which model runs at what effort. The first two are about oversight. The third is about how hard the model thinks. All three change in the session, in a few keystrokes, and the right setting changes with the task.

## Permission modes

A *permission mode* sets which actions the agent may take without asking you first. Every action an agent takes is one of four kinds: read a file, edit a file, run a command, or reach the network. The modes differ in which of those stop for a prompt. A prompt is a yes-or-no question in the session: *run this command?*, with the command shown.

In Claude Code, four modes are in everyday use. You cycle through them with `Shift+Tab` in the CLI; the desktop app has a mode selector, and the VS Code extension a mode indicator.

| Mode | What runs without asking | Best for |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Manual | Reads only. Every edit and every command prompts. | Your first sessions; anything near restricted data |
| Accept edits | Reads, file edits, and file housekeeping (`mkdir`, `mv`, `cp`) inside the project. Commands still prompt. | Everyday work you are reviewing as it goes |
| Plan | Reads and read-only commands. No edits until you approve a plan. | Any task whose shape is not obvious (next section) |
| Auto | Everything, with a second model (a *classifier*) reviewing each action against your request and blocking the ones it judges unsafe. | Long tasks with a plan, away from restricted data |

Which mode a session starts in depends on how you are signed in: on a personal Pro, Max, or Team plan it starts in Auto; on an Enterprise plan or through an institutional gateway it starts in Manual. Two further modes exist, *bypass permissions* and *don't ask*, which drop prompting entirely. The first is for isolated containers, the second for scripts. Neither belongs on a laptop with data on it, and you have to go out of your way to turn them on.

In Codex the setting is the `/permissions` picker, which offers three presets. Each bundles two dials: a *sandbox* (an operating-system fence around what a command can touch; §5) and an approval policy (when the agent stops to ask).

| Preset | What runs without asking | Best for |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Read-only | Reads. Every edit, command, and network request prompts. | Chatting about the project; planning; your first sessions |
| Auto | Reads, edits, and commands inside the project folder. Prompts before editing outside it or reaching the network. | Everyday work |
| Full Access | Everything: no sandbox, no prompts. Marked *not recommended* in the picker. | Nothing on a machine with data on it |

Codex picks its default sandbox from the folder: a folder under git starts in the workspace-write sandbox that Auto uses, a folder without git starts read-only. One more reason every project folder should be under version control (§5).

Three things to hold onto across both agents. First, a mode is a dial on prompts, not a fence. Deny rules (§5) block an action in every mode, whatever the agent or its classifier decides; the data rule for restricted paths belongs there, not in a mode. Second, the asymmetry: Claude Code hides its blanket bypass behind a launch flag, while Codex offers the equivalent as a preset. Do not pick it. Third, more prompts are not automatically safer. A session that asks forty questions trains you to answer yes without reading, and the click-fest that follows is a worse failure than a well-chosen Auto session (§5). The aim is a mode where every prompt you see is one you would actually read.

My own routine: Manual for the first sessions in a new project, until I have seen what it asks for. Accept edits for everyday work. Auto only when I am implementing a plan that came out of plan mode and no restricted data is in reach. I do not switch to Auto first and write the plan inside it.

## Plan mode

For any task whose shape is not obvious to both you and the agent before work starts, ask for a plan before any edits. Both agents build this in. In Claude Code, cycle to Plan with `Shift+Tab` (or pick it in the app's mode selector) and describe the task; in Codex, type `/plan` followed by the task. The agent reads what it needs to, drafts a step-by-step plan naming the files it intends to touch and the changes it intends to make, and waits. You edit the plan in place, then approve it, and only then does it start editing.

The payoff is catching the wrong-shaped solution at the plan stage instead of twenty file edits later. Even on tasks where you think the implementation is obvious, the plan surfaces assumptions the agent is making that you had not noticed: which files it considers in scope, which conventions it is inferring from your `AGENTS.md` and which from the surrounding code, what it intends to check when it is done, what it will do with the rows that do not merge. If a step is wrong, you change it. If the scope drifted, you narrow it. If something is unsafe, you strike it. None of that requires unwinding edits.

Plan mode for: reorganizing a folder into the paper shape (§7); writing the simulation study for a model (§12); converting an analysis to a second language (§13); anything touching `data/`. Not plan mode for: renaming a variable across scripts, fixing a typo, adding a missing `library()` call, copying a pattern from one script into another. The rule of thumb is that if the task is small and its shape is obvious to both of you, skip the plan; otherwise ask. The cost of asking when you did not need to is one round trip. The cost of not asking when you did is rework on a wrong-shaped solution, and a diff too large to review.

## Model and effort

Two settings change how the agent approaches a task, and both track how much of the approach is already known. The first is which *model* runs the job: both agents let you pick in the session, from the vendor's most capable model (the frontier model) down to a smaller, faster one. The second is *effort*: how much the model reasons before it acts.

In Claude Code, `/model` picks the model, by name or by family alias (`sonnet`, `opus`, `fable`), and `/effort` picks the level: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. The default is `high`; `max` is deliberately session-only and resets when you close the session. In Codex, one `/model` picker sets both the model and its reasoning effort, on a scale from `minimal` to `xhigh` depending on the model; `medium` is the usual starting point.

![](figures/two-gears.svg){#fig-two-gears fig-alt="Two coupled bars, model and effort, each ramping from left to right beneath a scale that runs from scripted work to open-ended work." above="6pt" below="6pt"}

Think of them as two gears that turn together with how scripted the task is. A deterministic recipe, such as scaffolding a project whose shape is already written down (§7) or applying a known pattern across scripts, runs well on a smaller model at lower effort: it thinks less and does more, and is faster for it. A job where the agent has to work out its own approach and change course as evidence arrives wants the frontier model and the depth. What links the two gears is a single dimension: how much of the approach is given, and how much the agent has to invent.

For research work the practical rule is simpler than the figure. Latency rarely matters; the real budget is your plan's usage allowance, which higher effort spends faster (§17). I pin both agents high and drop a session down when a task is clearly mechanical, rather than the reverse: a wrong turn on a statistical question costs more than the minutes saved. Two cautions. The names of the models change every few months, so treat the aliases as the stable part. And the top model tier may bill outside your plan's allowance (Claude Code says so in the `/model` picker when it does); check before an overnight run.
